title: Ashtpadi 6, salok: the thieves leave
hook: lust, anger, greed and attachment go, and pride too, by grace

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi five: the banker's capital, and a list of ten gifts. Your line was count the ten. Is the list still where you left it? Today, ashtpadi six begins. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

You may remember them from last year: the five thieves. Kaam, lust. Krodh, anger. Lobh, greed. Moh, attachment. Ahankaar, pride. The Guru Granth Sahib pictures them living inside the house of the body, quietly carrying off whatever is valuable. Last year we met them as a list. You probably also met them in your own life this week, maybe more than once. Ashtpadi six opens by naming them again, all five, in a single line. But this time the salok isn't describing the thieves. It's asking for something. And what it asks for is the surprise.
screen: `THE FIVE THIEVES, AGAIN.` → `LIVING IN THE HOUSE OF THE BODY.` → `THIS TIME, THE SALOK ASKS.`

segments.voice: The salok's first line lists them: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, and then ahanmev, which is pride, the sense of I alone, I myself. And it asks that they be destroyed, that they go. You might expect the second line to give a method. Five steps. A discipline for each thief. Instead the second line says: Nanak has come to God's sanctuary; bless me with Your grace, O divine Guru. The word for sanctuary is saranaagatee, coming for refuge, the way someone runs to a protected house when they're being chased. The word for grace is prasaad, a gift freely given. So the salok's answer to the five thieves isn't a fight in the dark. It's a door, and a request. Run to the house that's safe, and ask. That doesn't mean Sikhs sit back and do nothing. Elsewhere the Gurus speak of effort, of discipline, of living a disciplined, honest life, and the Sikh path is full of it. But this salok says something about where the change finally comes from. Pride can't be beaten by more pride, even pride in being humble. Anger can't be shouted down. The house is cleared by grace, coming in from outside. And that sets up the whole of ashtpadi six. Over the next three days it's going to repeat one phrase again and again: jih prasaad. By whose grace. The salok has just introduced the word.
screen: `LUST, ANGER, GREED, ATTACHMENT, PRIDE.` · `SARANAAGATEE: RUN FOR REFUGE.` · `PRASAAD: A GIFT FREELY GIVEN.` · `CLEARED FROM OUTSIDE, NOT FOUGHT.` · then, large: `GRACE CLEARS THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: breathe out one thief. Sit comfortably. Without judging yourself, let one of the five come to mind, the one that visited most this week. Lust, anger, greed, clinging, or pride. Just name it. Then breathe in slowly, as if the door of the house were opening. And as you breathe out, picture that thief walking out through it. You're not chasing it. You're making room. If you pray, you can ask for grace in your own way. Breathe in: open door. Breathe out: one thief leaves. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi six. Its salok names the five thieves, and asks for grace, prasaad, from the sanctuary of the Guru.
Your line: grace clears the house. Today, when one of the five shows up, don't wrestle it. Open a door: step outside, drink water, breathe once. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs name kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankaar as the five thieves, and in Sukhmani Sahib and the Ardas they ask for the Guru's grace and protection against them.

original.note: Gurmukhi: saranaagatee, coming to someone's protection for refuge; Nanak's answer to the five thieves.

trapdoor: what you thought: the thieves leave when you try hard enough.
what it means: the salok asks for grace to clear the house.
what a scholar hears: prasaad here sets up the refrain 'jih prasaad' (by whose grace) that runs through the stanzas of ashtpadi six.
